posts.title: Matter and Anti-Matter: Being Multiply Neurodivergent in Addiction and in Recovery
posts.excerpt: I spent the first eighteen years of my life feeling like a broken neurotypical.The most common thing I heard from teachers and professionals was that I was incredibly intelligent, but failing to meet my full potential. People expected great things of me. I could not see how to get there. I did not even know […]
posts.text:
I spent the first eighteen years of my life feeling like a broken neurotypical. The most common thing I heard from teachers and professionals was that I was incredibly intelligent, but failing to meet my full potential. People expected great things of me. I could not see how to get there. I did not even know what it was that was expected of me; only that, whatever it was, I was not managing it.

Underneath that was a great deal of childhood trauma, and an Autistic ADHD neurocognitive style that nobody had named. My mental health was declining rapidly. I was hearing voices and living with paranoia. The institutions and power structures around me would not acknowledge my needs, let alone accommodate them.

That is the ecosystem I was using drugs and alcohol in. I think we have to start there, because almost every conversation about addiction starts at the crash, and by then the most important part of the story has already happened.

What The Drugs Were Actually Doing

Substances were not a failure of character. They were a solution, and for a long time they were an extremely effective one.
They made the burden lighter; they quietened the hallucinations and stopped me circling my paranoia, regulated my sensory environment for me when nothing else would, and they gave me a relational world, a community of other users where we could bond over the ridiculous things that happened while we were drunk and high, seek out and experiment with whatever we could acquire, and, together, discover that human consciousness was boundless.

They also gave me something I have only been able to articulate since; a legible identity. When I behaved neurodivergently, people attributed it to the drugs rather than to difference. David the drug user was more acceptable to the world than David the Neurodivergent person. Which is absurd when you think about it, that is an entire society telling you which version of yourself it is prepared to tolerate.

More than anything, though, they took the soul-crushing feelings of fear and failure and turned them off. A line, a pill, a pipe, and it all melted away almost instantly. My fear of dying is really a fear of oblivion, and substances handed me agency over that oblivion; I could choose it, in doses, on my terms.

If you are trying to understand why someone uses, that is the question to sit with. Not “why can’t they stop”, but “what is this doing that nothing else in their life is doing”.

The Turn

I did not notice the change as it happened. It was fast, but it was subtle, looking back, I can trace it to my lung collapsing when I was twenty-two. A spontaneous pneumothorax, brought on by everything I had smoked, and by being tall and underweight, which is a significant risk factor in itself.

While I was recovering from that I developed pneumonia and pleurisy, and I was prescribed tramadol for the pain. I remember the first dose exactly; it was like being wrapped in a warm, cosy blanket and looking out at the world through rose-tinted glasses. It was perfection.

Around the same time, my psychiatrist put me on diazepam.
I want to be careful here, because this is the part of my story that people find least comfortable. My addiction did not escalate because street dealers got to me. It escalated because medicine handed me a better, cleaner, more reliable version of the solution I had already found. By the end I was taking over 200mg of diazepam a day alongside lorazepam, clonazepam and etizolam, drinking liquid morphine and oxycodone like soft drinks, and adding whatever else I could get hold of. What I could not get prescribed, I sourced illicitly. I became genuinely skilled at managing doctors into giving me what I wanted.

My life became an experiment. I kept detailed journals of what I had taken, in what quantities, in what combinations, and what it did. I was chasing an idealised state of consciousness, a precise point where my mind was in just enough oblivion to forget how frightened of dying I was. I woke up every day and tried to induce myself into a coma, somewhere between the world of the living and no longer existing.

Pieces Of Descartes’ Machinery

The obvious question is how nobody noticed. The UK medical system is the opposite of holistic. It is a series of experts in very specific pieces of Descartes’ machinery, each of them rarely looking beyond their own piece. Nobody was holding the whole picture, and that was the opening. The fragmentation of my care created the exact conditions in which I could present whatever each service needed to see in order to give me what I wanted.

I did not outwit a joined-up system, I moved through the gaps in a disjointed one. It was only when I finally recognised that I needed help that the parts began to join up at all, and even then it took years before anyone took the bodymind approach that would actually get me near recovery.

Matter And Anti-Matter

The first time I knew I was in serious trouble was when I stole my mother’s post-operative oxycodone prescription to stop myself going into withdrawal. Around then I also started having frequent seizures, most likely because I was smoking around seven grams of spice a day on top of everything else. So I asked for help. What happened? Substance use services told me they could not treat me effectively while my extensive mental health needs went unmet. Mental health services labelled me with a personality disorder and told me they would not work with me until I stopped using.

Those two services behaved like matter and anti-matter. They annihilated each other on contact, and took my hope of recovery with them. It is worth saying plainly what that label meant in context. An undiagnosed Autistic, ADHD man with a substantial trauma history, in acute distress, presenting in ways nobody had the framework to read, was recorded as having a disordered personality. Not an unmet need, nor a nervous system under siege. A disordered personality. I know how many people reading this will recognise themselves in that sentence.

Waking Up In Resus

Two things eventually broke the deadlock. The first was a good care co-ordinator who pushed services to take responsibility for their part, even when they only did so minimally. Never underestimate what one person willing to make a nuisance of themselves can hold open.

The second was a huge overdose and seizure. I woke up in the resuscitation area of my local emergency department. I was discharged, went home, told my mother and my sister I was going into detox, and phoned my key worker at the substance use service. Within a week I was an inpatient on the detox ward of the local psychiatric hospital. That was the point at which the true extent of the mental health damage became fully visible. I did a further six months of community detox, and my first day of recovery was the 7th of April 2016.

Thirty days later I had my first full psychotic episode, and spent another month as a psychiatric inpatient. That episode lasted several

posts.title: Ecosystemic Distress and the Limits of Criminal Defences
posts.excerpt: Since psychologically distressed states and criminality are so entwined in the literature, then when behaviour is criminalised, we arrive at a collision. The law wants to know what was in your head. The ecosystemic account says; look at what your head was in.
posts.text:
The law needs a culprit. Criminal law has a job to do, and that job requires an individual. It requires a person who intended an outcome, or foresaw an outcome, or whom caused an outcome through negligence. Someone who can therefore be held to account for it. The entire apparatus, actus reus, mens rea, the defences that sit around them, is a machine for locating responsibility inside a single body and then acting on that body.

This is not incidental to the law, rather it is the law’s founding assumption. This is precisely the assumption the Ecosystemic Model of Distress and Wellbeing was built to dismantle . Not that criminal responsibility is a falsehood, but that criminal acts do not occur in isolation . Even those who can not use such a defence as “…by reason of insanity” can still have their criminal behaviour understood within it’s ecosystemic context.

The ecosystemic position is straightforward; distress is an output, rather than an intrinsic property of a person. It emerges from the interaction between a bodymind and the complex and dynamic environments it exists in relation to.

The immediate sensory and relational environment, the institutional environment of school and service and workplace, and the structural environment of policy, economy, and the neuronormative expectations that saturate all of it. Distress is what happens when those environments demand something a bodymind cannot sustainably give. As opposed to having a specific location, it is the sum of the whole arrangement .

If that is true of distress, then it is also true of behaviour. Since psychologically distressed states and criminality are so entwined in the literature, then when behaviour is criminalised, we arrive at a collision. The law wants to know what was in your head. The ecosystemic account says; look at what your head was in . This, it could be argued, begins to move us away from criminal justice and towards a model by which we can actively work to prevent crime in the first place.

Autistic Mental Health Conference 2026 On-Demand

What The Defences Will And Will Not Hear

The thing that should trouble anyone reading criminal defences through an ecosystemic lens is that the law is not entirely deaf to the argument that a person’s capacity was compromised: it has a whole vocabulary for it. However, it will only listen if the compromise is relocated inside the person. It fails to acknowledge the complex cultural and ecosystemic variables that create the context for the crime to occur in in the first place.

• Insanity in England and Wales still runs on the M’Naghten Rules of 1843; a defect of reason, arising from disease of the mind.

• Diminished responsibility under the amended Homicide Act requires an abnormality of mental functioning arising from a recognised medical condition.

• Automatism turns on whether the cause was internal or external, which is why a diabetic’s criminal liability can depend on whether they took their insulin or didn’t . The US position varies by state, but the M’Naghten test dominates there too, and since 2020 a state is free to abolish the insanity defence altogether and permit mental illness only to negate the mental element.

Every single one of these demands the same trade; you may have your reduced culpability, but you must accept a pathologising account of yourself to get it . The law will hear “my brain was disordered”, however, It will not hear “my life was disordered”.

This is the bind, and it is a familiar one to anyone who has fought for support in the SEND system or through adult mental health services. Access to accommodation is gated behind diagnosis; access to mercy is gated behind pathology . In both cases you are handed a script written by someone else and told that speaking it is the price of being heard at all.

Fricker’s testimonial injustice is doing a lot of work here, the defendant’s own account of why they did what they did carries no evidential weight until a psychiatrist restates it in the language of disorder . The expert is the credible speaker, the person is a set of symptoms with a mouth.

Foucault would recognise this immediately. The insanity defence is not a mercy mechanism, it is a sorting mechanism. It separates the mad from the bad, and it does so on terms set by the institutions that will subsequently manage whichever category you land in. Prison or hospital order, either way, you are dealt with.

The Exceptions That Prove The Rule

The law is not wholly incapable of recognising that circumstances compel, however it recognises it in a very particular shape. Duress admits that a person can be so constrained by their situation that blame is inappropriate ; though it should be noted that case law has historically set the conditions tightly:

• A threat of death or serious injury

• No safe avenue of escape,

Critically, the defence is unavailable to anyone who voluntarily associated with criminals when they could have foreseen coercion . Section 45 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 does something similar for people compelled to offend through trafficking or slavery.

So the law will accept ecosystemic compulsion when it takes the form of a specific person making a specific threat, but what it will not accept is diffuse structural coercion. There is no defence of poverty or of having been excluded from education at nine, restrained through your adolescence, and left without a single functioning support relationship by the time you were an adult . There is no defence of being a monotropic bodymind in an environment engineered to produce monotropic split, sustained in that state for two decades, and then criminalised for what the resulting distress made of you.

This is the sharpest critique of criminal justice provided by ecological models. The law punishes people for the ecosystem they were placed in. If you grew up somewhere where the only available relational network was a criminal one (because that was what the neighbourhood contained, because that was who would have you, because every legitimate institution had already excluded you) the law treats your presence in that network as a free choice that forfeits the defence of coercion . It reads adaptation to a hostile environment as complicity in it.

The same logic governs intoxication. Some case law holds that voluntary intoxication is no answer to a basic intent crime, with some cases law confirming that a drugged intent is still an intent. In the US, case law upheld a state’s power to exclude intoxication evidence entirely. Addiction is thereby constituted as a series of freely made choices, the first of which contaminates all the rest.

English law will allow alcohol dependence syndrome to assert diminished responsibility, but only for murder, and only once psychiatry has certified the dependency as a disease. Again, the pathology toll has to be paid. Your compulsion is legible only after it has been medicalised .

posts.title: What Does Autism Feel Like?
posts.excerpt: I am Autistic. I know this, not only because I was diagnosed after extensive assessment, but also because of my feeling of belonging within the Autistic cultural ecosystem. I am, however, plagued by a question that I am yet to find a satisfactory answer to: What does autism feel like?
posts.text:
I am Autistic. I know this, not only because I was diagnosed after extensive assessment, but also because of my feeling of belonging within the Autistic cultural ecosystem. I am, however, plagued by a question that I am yet to find a satisfactory answer to:

Do I feel Autistic?

The Nature Of Being Autistic

Autism itself is not a physical entity. There is no object of any kind that one could point to and claim “this is autism”. We know of autism through the existence of Autistic people, and yet, there is still no unanimous consensus on the semiotic nature of Autistic people’s existence.

We exist to symbolise autism, and yet no one can agree on an autism proper.

Autistic people connect and come to know their autism through cultural exchange and symbolic recognition; we know our own. We can agree that our experience is an Autistically experienced one, but only through our shared reference points with other Autistic people.

Phenomenology Of Autism

From a phenomenological perspective, we can describe how we feel as an Autistic individual, but could not tell what it is about that feeling that is “autism”.

I, as an Autistic person, have no point of reference within a non-Autistic experience. I was born Autistic, I am Autistic, and I will die Autistic. To give a true phenomenological account of how autism feels I would first need to feel something non-Autistic to contrast the experience with.

This in itself is the root of the double empathy problem. Where experiences of the ecosystem we inhabit depart too much from those of the people we try to communicate with, our inability to impart more than a hypothetical understanding of what it feels like to be us causes mutual degradation of empathy and subsequent attempts at communication.

I can’t say that I feel Autistic, I can say that I feel like me . I can also say that I relate to the feelings of other people who identify with the Autistic identifier. It would seem to me that Autistic experience is a fundamentally cultural/ecological one. Our knowledge of our Autistic selves is constructed through our interaction with the human ecosystem. Since my experience of said ecosystem aligns with the collective agreement of other Autistic people sharing that space, I can then know I am Autistic.

Those external to the Autistic cultural experience are then left in the position of having to trust my assertion that I am Autistic. Sadly, ideology and hermeneutical injustice often render assertion invalid.

What Does This Mean For Autistic People?

The immediate rebuttal that I anticipate is from those who would claim that individuals with more observably profound degrees of support needs can not be a part of such a cultural space and thus they would assert a division between Autistic people like myself, who can articulate themselves freely, and those whom require 24 hour care.

I would respond by noting that human cultures throughout time have contained individuals with varying degrees of support needs, including those most profoundly marginalised. It is not that we should see their autism as different to my autism.

The question I would pose is whether or not our emergent Autistic culture is accessible to all Autistic people, and why Autistic people are so frequently categorised by the support they require. It would seem to me that a better use of time would be to improve quality of life for all Autistic people within the ecosystem.

My next point is this; if Autistic experience is an ecologically grown cultural one, then the systematic ignorance of Autistic individuals on matters pertaining to the identification and support of Autistic people is an ideological choice rather than a valid account of who is and is not Autistic. Autistic experience frequently includes an insistence on denying the Autistic person.

So, to answer the titular question, which is the reason you have read this article (and kudos if you have made it thus far); being Autistic feels like being me. Autistic people are human beings, therefore to be Autistic is to feel human. The main difference in my Autistically human experience is societies incessant need to make me feel non-human.

Who I am, and what I will become, is a function of my Autistic nature (in all of it’s symbolic glory) in relation to the ecosystem I inhabit, and the cultural spaces I frequent. I am no more or less Autistic than any other Autistic person, and yet, to be Autistic is to know that my Autistic experience symbolises just one thread in a tapestry of Autistic life on this planet.

posts.title: Why We Held An Autistic Mental Health Conference
posts.excerpt: An exploration of why we held an Autistic Mental Health Conference.
posts.text:
The world of academia and knowledge-production is renowned for it’s disinterest in lived experience. While it is true that anecdotes are almost impossible to generalise in the statistical sense, the positioning of external observation by a meritocratic expert as being above that of the experience of the subject of observation represents an ethical dilemma that has plagued not only academia but also the people being observed for many years.

Autistic people are a classic example of a group that is often spoken about rather than spoken to . This is why we held an Autistic Mental Health Conference. Marilyn Charles writes in their essay Madness And Mysticism in the anthology The Entanglement Of Culture And Psychosis (Lambrecht & Lavis, 2026):

Knowing about is not the same as knowing

This is itself the basis of Milton’s Double Empathy Problem. Deficits in empathy, through this framing, can be seen as mutual experiential mismatch rather than deficits.

I, as an Autistic man, can not personally understand a non-Autistic man’s experience, and therefore can only “ know about ” non-Autistic experience and not “ know ” it. However, this is not because i lack empathy for the non-Autistic man in question, I can empathise quite well with other Autistic people. The non-Autistic man in question experiences the same in reverse.

It should be noted that the double empathy problem could succesfully be applied to any experiential difference. Professional to non-professional. Cis-gender man to woman or gender diverse person. White person to Black person. We can not know what we don’t experience. At best we can know about , which is perceptibly superficial at best.

So, why did we hold the Autistic Mental Health Conference? Autistic people are often victims of epistemic injustice. Our accounts of our experience are seen as invalid or untrustworthy. For me, it would seem that two things form the basis of this epistemic injustice, first would be Yergeau’s demi-rhetoricity; we are both too Autistic and not Autistic enough to have a trusted voice on autism. The second is that those who know about autism are gifted a meritocratic superiority over the people who know what it is to be Autistic.

The Autistic Mental Health Conference took a different approach, however. We platformed Autistic people who know Autistic experience. That doesn’t mean that we were able to encompass all Autistic experience. What it does mean is that we shifted the power balance away from those who know about autism towards those who know for three days, on an international platform.

This was important for more than just reasons of being Autistic. Autistic people are more likely to experience mental health concerns with some research suggesting a prevalence of 8 in 10 people in the Autistic population compared to 1 in 4 in the general population. Further to this, Autistic experiences of mental health and it’s associated happenings often depart from those of non-Autistic people.

This presents a nuance that a non-Autistic expert can know about , but only the Autistic person can truly know . Given the rates of negative experiences, amounting to significantly increased suicide risk, it is vital that we primarily platform the people who know over the people who know about .

It’s not that academic expertise does not have value, it’s that expertise in the absence of the context of lived experience is similar to learning to speak a language but never visiting the country where it is natively spoken.

The Autistic Mental Health Conference aimed to bring that Autistic lived experience, the culture that underlies that experience, to the forefront. It was a demonstration of the collective impact that Autistic people have when given the platform to voice their experiences and be heard. That is why we held this conference .

posts.title: Your Mental Health Was Never Just Yours
posts.excerpt: There’s a question I’ve been asking for years, and I want to ask it here before I tell you anything about conference tickets or timings: Who taught you that your distress was your fault? Because someone did. Maybe it was a clinician who told you your anxiety was a “feature of your autism”, or a […]
posts.text:
There’s a question I’ve been asking for years, and I want to ask it here before I tell you anything about conference tickets or timings:

Who taught you that your distress was your fault?

Because someone did. Maybe it was a clinician who told you your anxiety was a “feature of your autism”, or a school that called your child’s shutdown “behaviour”, perhaps it was a workplace that offered you a wellbeing app whilst refusing to turn the lights down; it could even have been you, at 3am, deciding that the problem must be you because everyone keeps saying so.

The 2026 Autistic Mental Health Conference exists because I don’t believe that story. Neither does anyone speaking at it.

The Theme: Ecosystemic Causes Of Mental Health Issues

Three days. 14th–16th August. The whole event is built around one argument; Autistic distress is not a symptom of being Autistic, it is a response to environments and systems that were never built for us.

That is a structural claim. If distress is ecosystemic, then individual treatment alone will always be insufficient; the school, the workplace, the benefits system, the therapy room and the family home are all clinical sites. If distress is ecosystemic, then a lot of professionals are going to have to change what they do.

Tanya Adkin and I will be presenting the Ecosystemic Model of Distress on Friday afternoon, the framework we’ve spent years developing to explain this, but we’re one talk out of dozens.

Who else is speaking

Dr. Nick Walker on unorthodox approaches to Autistic psychological resilience. If you’ve read Neuroqueer Heresies , you know why this matters.

Natasha Leahy on late identification as systemic harm: the trauma of not knowing.

Dr. Nathan Keates on power and meaning in Autistic mental distress.

Ava McAuley on masking, the Double Empathy Problem, and why burnout isn’t a personal failure.

Erin Ekins on growing up queerly Autistic: fresh from the BBC after her book was at the centre of a school ban.

Meryem Cetinkaya on autism, suicidality, and co-created care.

Karen Parker on the “performance over health” school culture that breaks children before anyone intervenes.

Jessica Dark on workplace stress as an organisational design problem, not an employee problem.

Emily Nuttall on AuDHD, eating disorders, trauma and addiction — lived experience, unflinching.

Plus Jess Nicks, Lawrence Kampf, Sarah Meharg, Ed Shearer, Nic James, Nikki Smith, Stacy Badon, Amber Dawn, Harry Mansfield, and an entire on-demand library of talks we couldn’t fit into the schedule. In total there are more than 20 speakers.

Every one of them neurodivergent or working directly alongside neurodivergent communities. This is a conference about us, by us.

What it costs, and how to get in

We built this hybrid on purpose, because an inaccessible conference about accessibility is a joke.

NeuroHub Community members get 33% off every ticket. Membership is free. Join the community , contact our admin team for your code, use it at checkout. There is no catch and no reason not to.

Friday and Sunday are online. Saturday is live in Brighton with stalls, food and entertainment; and livestreamed for everyone who can’t travel. All talks are recorded and available to ticket holders afterwards for 6 months, so if your capacity collapses on day two, you haven’t lost anything.

Get your ticket here

Now the part I actually want from you

I don’t want you to read this and quietly close the tab; I want a discussion, so:

1. What’s the single environmental thing that damages your mental health most; and what would it take to change it? Not the diagnosis. the thing. The open-plan office, the school run, the DWP letter. Name it.

2. Professionals: what were you taught about Autistic mental health that you’ve since had to unlearn? I’ll go first; I was taught that distress was a deficit to be managed. It isn’t, it’s information about the environment.

3. Parents: when did you first realise the system was going to make you fight for basic humanity?

4. What talk isn’t on our programme that should be? We’re already thinking about next year.

Drop your answers in the comments. Post them on your own feeds., tag us. Share this post with the one person who keeps insisting your burnout is a personal resilience problem.

We’ve got five days. The conversation starts now, and it doesn’t stop when the last session ends on Sunday.

See you there.

posts.title: The “Overdiagnosis” Review: What It Actually Means for Autistic People and Their Families
posts.excerpt: The UK’s overdiagnosis review explained: what it actually found, and what it could mean for your autism assessment, PIP claim, EHCP and workplace adjustments
posts.text:
If you are Autistic, waiting for an assessment, or supporting an Autistic child, you have probably seen the headlines. People “incentivised” to get diagnoses, an overdiagnosis crisis, a government review questioning whether autism and ADHD is being handed out too freely.

It is unsettling reading, and a lot of it is framing rather than fact. This piece is not about who is right in that argument, instead I want to ask something more useful; what is actually happening, what could realistically change, and what it means in practice for your assessment, your benefits, your child’s school place, and your job.

What Is Actually Happening

In December 2025, the Department of Health and Social Care commissioned an independent review into the prevalence of, and support for, mental health conditions, ADHD, and autism. Professor Peter Fonagy chairs it, with Professor Sir Simon Wessely and Professor Gillian Baird as vice-chairs. An interim report was published on GOV.UK in June 2026, and a final report is expected during 2026.

The terms of reference ask the review to look at the factors behind trends in prevalence, the impact of clinical practice including “the risks and benefits of medicalisation”, prevention and early intervention, and different models of support both within and beyond the NHS.

Running alongside it is the Timms Review; the first full review of Personal Independence Payment since PIP was introduced. It reports to the Secretary of State in autumn 2026. The two are connected, with findings from the health review expected to feed into the benefits review.

That connection is the reason this matters practically rather than just intellectually. A debate about diagnostic thresholds in a medical journal is limited in the scope of immediate change that it precipitates. A debate about diagnostic thresholds that lands on the desk of a benefits review three months before eligibility rules are rewritten is a different thing entirely.

What The Interim Report Actually Said

On common mental health conditions (mainly anxiety and depression) the review found evidence of a real increase in population prevalence over the past two decades, particularly among younger people. Prevalence among 16 to 64 year olds rose from around 15.5% in 1993 to around 22.6% in 2023-24.

On autism and ADHD, it found something different. The best population data suggests underlying prevalence has been relatively stable, while diagnoses and referrals have risen dramatically. Thirteen times more people were waiting for an autism assessment in September 2025 than in April 2019.

Critically, the review did not conclude from this that the extra diagnoses are false. It said several processes are likely operating at once;

• Genuine changes in distress

• Better recognition of need that was previously missed

• Changes in help-seeking

• Changes in professional and public understanding

• Institutional incentives attached to holding a diagnosis.

That last item is what the press picked up, but it is one factor in a list, and it describes a system problem, not a patient problem. If support is only available to people with a diagnosis, people will pursue a diagnosis, that is the system working exactly as designed.

This is also consistent with the existing research. A UK cohort study found a 787% increase in recorded autism diagnoses between 1998 and 2018, with the sharpest rises among adults and among women and girls, the groups historically missed. A separate Lancet Regional Health (Europe) study of GP records in England concluded that Autistic adults remain substantially underdiagnosed and that policies aimed at fixing this have not yet worked. Both findings can be true at once; recorded diagnoses rising steeply, and a large number of Autistic people still undiagnosed.

The interim report’s own direction of travel is towards a system that is, in Fonagy’s phrase, “more proportionate, more responsive and less dependent on diagnosis alone.”

Where The Risk Sits

Needs-led support instead of diagnosis-gated support is, on its face, what most Autistic advocates have wanted for years. A diagnosis should not be the turnstile you have to pass through to get a quiet room, a later start time, or help with paperwork.

The concern raised by organisations across the sector is about sequencing and framing. Removing the diagnostic gate is good if you build the support first, removing it while questioning whether the diagnoses were valid, during a period of pressure on welfare spending, produces fewer routes in, and less legitimacy for the people already through the door.

That is the thing to watch. Not “will they abolish autism” (they will not) but whether support arrives before the gate is narrowed.

Five Practical Areas, And What Could Actually Change

1. Getting an assessment

This is where pressure is already visible, and it predates the review.

As of March 2026 there were 270,701 people with an open referral for suspected autism in England, and around 90% had been waiting longer than the 13 weeks NICE recommends. Right to Choose (the mechanism that lets you ask for referral to any qualifying provider with an NHS contract) has been restricted in practice by a growing number of Integrated Care Boards since 2024, through capped provider panels, prior-approval requirements and GP guidance discouraging its use.

Legally, ICBs cannot abolish Right to Choose by policy; the NHS Standard Contract still requires them to comply with patient choice obligations. In practice, availability varies enormously depending on where you live.

Some areas are also moving to needs-led models. Greater Manchester introduced a new model of care from January 2026 focused on getting people support based on individual need rather than diagnosis alone, with coaching, peer groups and self-help offered while people wait.

What this means for you: if you are considering an assessment, the practical case for starting the process sooner rather than later is stronger than it was a year ago, not because diagnosis is about to disappear, but because routes in are being narrowed locally and the waiting lists are long. Check your own ICB’s current Right to Choose position rather than assuming national guidance applies to you.

2. PIP and benefits

The proposal to require four or more points in a single daily living activity was dropped after significant opposition, but the powers may still be applied to new claimants from November 2026, once the Timms Review reports.

The picture on who is affected is genuinely mixed, and it is worth considering both halves. DWP’s own analysis suggested that people with physical conditions such as back pain and arthritis would be most affected by the four-point change, and that people with learning disabilities, autism and ADHD would be least likely to be affected (because Autistic claimants often score across several activities rather than heavily in one). posts.title: Why Neurodivergent Community Matters For Neurodivergent People
posts.excerpt: Why Neurodivergent Community is important and where you can find it.
posts.text:
It’s no secret to the neurodivergent community at large that performing a neurocognitive style that differs from the neuronormative standard of our given culture is a challenge that is often overlooked. For many of us, the only exception to the constant barrage of complaints on how we exist can be found in neurodivergent community, created by and for us. It isn’t that the only way to thrive is to isolate ourselves from the world, rather that such spaces offer a meaningful place to experience the lack of barriers that typical society simply doesn’t offer.

Neurodivergent Community & Mental Health

Neurodivergent people perform differently from neurotypical society, and as a result experience an increased amount of stigma, discrimination, and even vulnerability to criminal exploitation and violence. It is no surprise, then, that spaces where we can connect with each other in solidarity have an overall positive impact on our mental health.

Such spaces create the opportunity to engage with others in a meaningful way without the threat of critical opinions or overt disregard for our humanity. They create a reprieve from the constant barrage of “you are not enough”, “you are too much”, or “how can I take advantage of you?” that we experience on a more or less daily basis. This allows us to experience human connection without the constant threat of mistreatment.

Where Is The Neurodivergent Community?

Below are a few examples of creators and professionals building community on both social media and other platforms where you can connect with other Autistic and neurodivergent people.

Autistic Realms

Autistic Realms is run by Helen Edgar, who herself is our communications and partnership lead here at NeuroHub Community. Helen works tirelessly to create content, connect neurodivergent people with each other, and advance the knowledge that we hold about what it is to be neurodivergent.

Autistic Inclusive Meets

Autistic Inclusive Meets is a community group in London that not only provides a number of in-person meet-up and event opportunities but also engages in critical activism to protect Autistic people from abuse and quack treatments. Their CEO Emma Dalmayne has a global platform of work and has locked horns with some of the biggest threats to Autistic people that have existed in recent decades.

Autistic Parents UK

Autistic Parents UK provide community and support for Autistic parents across the United Kingdom. There work provides meaningful support and community for a group fo parents that are not only often overlooked, but frequently mistreated by professional services.

Jade Farrington

Jade Farrignton is a neurodivergent therapist who is well known for their comprehensive newsletter, helping connect neurodivergent people with services, events, and each other. You can check out her newsletter by clicking the button below.

Jade’s Newsletter

Ausome Minds

Ausome Minds is the organisation run by Charlie Hart (AKA Ausome Charlie) providing professional speaking and training services with a particular focus on LGBTQIA+ intersections with neurodiversity. Ausome Minds is also a sponsor of NeuroHub Community and have done a lot to support our work.

Neurodivergent Joy

Neurodivergent Joy is run by Ed Shearer and is an emerging body of work providing professional speaking, training and consultancy across the world of autism and neurodiversity. I would highly recommend checking our Ed’s work and supporting the growth of his endeavours.

Visit The Website

This list will continue to grow as the team here at NeuroHub Community have time to invest in adding more to it. If you’re not on here yet, don’t worry, you soon will be, and you can always get in contact with us at admin@neurohubcommunity.org to let us know about your work!

Autistic Mental Health Conference 2026

posts.title: Why Gang Culture Can Be Attractive to Autistic People
posts.excerpt: An exploration of what os attractive for Autistic people about gang culture and some points on how to support Autistic people on how to leave gang life.
posts.text:
Gang involvement among Autistic people is rarely discussed in neurodivergent-affirming spaces, and when it is discussed at all, it tends to be framed through a criminological or risk-management lens rather than a relational one. This article takes a different starting point; it asks not “how do we stop Autistic people joining gangs” but “what need is the gang meeting, and why is it meeting it better than anything else on offer”. Until we answer that question honestly, any intervention we design will fail.

Minority Stress And Marginalisation

Autistic people are a minoritised group, and like other minoritised groups, we experience minority stress; that is, chronic stress arising specifically from occupying a stigmatised social position, over and above the general stressors of everyday life.

Economic Marginalisation

Autistic adults face some of the worst employment outcomes of any disabled group in the UK. Workplaces are rarely designed with monotropic attention, sensory difference, or communication difference in mind, and disclosure frequently leads to discrimination rather than accommodation. The result is chronic under-employment, in-work poverty, and exclusion from the economic structures that most people rely on for stability and status.

Social Marginalisation

Social marginalisation compounds this. The double empathy problem means Autistic people are routinely misread by non-autistic peers, leading to exclusion, bullying, and a lifetime of relationships that fail before they properly begin.

Many Autistic people arrive at adolescence and adulthood having never experienced sustained, reciprocal peer connection; this is not because we do not want connection, but because the social world around us has consistently failed to meet us halfway.

Community Connectedness As A Buffer

Dr Monique Botha’s 2020 doctoral research, along with their paper with David Frost extending the minority stress model to autistic populations, demonstrated that minority stress is a substantial and independent contributor to poor mental health in Autistic people; discrimination, stigma, and concealment all predicted worse outcomes, regardless of other factors.

Critically, Botha’s wider body of work showed that autistic community connectedness; a felt sense of belonging to a shared psychological space with other Autistic people, acts as a buffer against these effects.

Where connectedness is present, the mental health impact of minority stress is significantly reduced.
This finding matters enormously for understanding gang involvement; if connectedness to a community of belonging is what protects against the harm of marginalisation, then any group offering that connectedness, regardless of what else it involves, will be psychologically compelling to someone who is starved of it elsewhere.

Grooming, Trafficking, And Vulnerability

It is important to be direct about how many Autistic people enter gang life in the first place; it is very often not a free choice made from a position of options, but a process of grooming and exploitation that specifically targets vulnerability.

Autistic traits that are otherwise framed as deficits by services (literal interpretation of language, a strong drive toward rule-following once rules are established and logically internalised, difficulty reading manipulative intent, a desperate hunger for consistent social contact) are precisely the traits that make a person easier to groom.

Perpetrators offer attention, purpose, and unconditional-seeming acceptance to young people who have rarely experienced any of the three; only once trust and dependency are established does exploitation begin, frequently through county lines trafficking, debt bondage, or coercive control dressed up as loyalty. This is criminal exploitation of a disabled young person, and it should be named as such; the young person is a victim of trafficking before they are ever a participant in crime.

Gang Life As Family Structure

For those who remain within it past the initial grooming, gang life is frequently experienced and described in the language of family; hierarchy, loyalty, ritual, discipline, and unconditional-in-theory belonging. This is not incidental, gangs deliberately structure themselves as surrogate kinship systems, because kinship is what recruits are missing.

Like any family, this comes with the best and worst of what family life contains. There is genuine care, shared history, protection, and a felt sense of being known. There is also control, violence, conditional love, and the kind of harm that families are also capable of producing. For an Autistic person who has never had a stable family or peer structure, the presence of both is still preferable to the absence of either; a flawed, sometimes dangerous form of belonging can feel safer than a non-Autistic world that offers no belonging at all.

Crime as the Side Effect, Not the Point

This reframing matters clinically and practically; for many Autistic members, the criminal activity is not the draw. It is the toll paid for access to the family structure, not the reason for joining it. The monotropic pull is toward the relationship, the routine, the role, and the certainty of the hierarchy; the criminal element is a side section engaged with in order to keep the connection, rather than the connection existing in order to facilitate crime.

This distinction changes how we should think about intervention entirely. Punitive approaches that focus on the crime miss the actual mechanism holding the person in place, and often deepen the very isolation that made the gang attractive to begin with.

Moving Away from Gang Life:

• Replacing the Social Circle

• If connectedness is the mechanism, then connectedness must be the intervention. Removing an Autistic person from a gang without replacing the social circle it provided simply recreates the original conditions of minority stress, unmitigated by any buffer; this is why so many exit attempts fail or result in reoffending.

• Effective support has to include:

• Building a genuine Autistic-community-connected social circle before or alongside disengagement, so the person is not moved from one form of belonging into a vacuum

• Explicit education on what a healthy family or relationship looks like, delivered in a way that accounts for autistic experience rather than assuming neurotypical relational models transfer directly

• Trauma-informed recognition that the person is a survivor of exploitation, not simply a former offender

• Long-term relational continuity, since trust, once built with genuine community, is what the gang exploited in the first place, and it cannot be rebuilt on a short intervention timescale

Conclusion

Gang culture is not attractice to Autistic people because we are drawn to crime; it is attractive because it offers, however conditionally, the community-connectedness that Botha’s research shows we need to survive minority stress, and that the rest of soc

posts.title: The Bleach They Call A Miracle: Chlorine Dioxide, Fake Cures, And The War On Autistic Existence

posts.text:
I need to start with the thing that should be the headline, not the footnote; parents are giving children bleach. Not as a metaphor or hyperbole. Actual bleach, administered by mouth and by enema, on a schedule some of them time to the phases of the moon. They are doing it because they have been told, by people who present themselves as healers, that this is how you get rid of an Autistic child and get a “recovered” one back.

I am not interested in softening that sentence for you. The Ecosystemic Model has taught me that distress is never just personal, it’s structural; but sometimes the structure is a bottle of industrial bleach sold through a Telegram channel, and the ecosystem is a parent’s terror weaponised for profit. Let’s take this apart properly.

What Chlorine Dioxide Actually Is

Chlorine dioxide is not some obscure “alternative” compound. It’s an industrial bleaching agent, most commonly used in water treatment and paper pulp processing. When sold as “Miracle Mineral Solution” (MMS), “CD”, “CDS”, or “Water Purification Solution”, it’s typically a sodium chlorite solution that the buyer is instructed to mix with a citric acid activator that when added to the mixture becomes chlorine dioxide, a powerful bleaching agent ( Disability Scoop, 2019 ) . There is no reframing of that chemistry that makes it something other than what it is. It is bleach, it was never not bleach.

Who Started Feeding This To Autistic Children

The origin story matters, because it tells you everything about the epistemics of this movement. MMS was first promoted roughly twenty years ago as a remedy for nearly every ailment by a former Scientologist who went on to found a “church of health and healing” called Genesis II ( NBC News ); that man is Jim Humble, and I want you to sit with the fact that he has claimed, in his own videos, to be a billion-year-old god from the Andromeda galaxy ( ABC7 News ) . This is the foundational figure of the movement that later got aimed at Autistic children.

The person who did the aiming was Kerri Rivera, a former real estate agent from Chicago ( NBC News ) with no medical training, who relocated her operation to Mexico and began counselling parents of Autistic children on a “miracle treatment” she claimed could rid their children of what she called “the curse” ( NBC Chicago ) of autism. Rivera folded chlorine dioxide into a wider “CD protocol” that also involves a strict diet and instructions for parents to watch for the “purging” of parasites from their children’s bodies ( NBC Chicago ) , and she has claimed the protocol has removed more than 170 children from the autism spectrum ( NBC Chicago ) . She has also framed autism itself as vaccine injury (Substack) , which tells you she is not operating from one piece of misinformation but from an entire alternate epistemology built to justify the next one.

What should chill you more than the individual biography is the theology underneath it. Rivera’s protocol timed doses to the full moon, on the claim that parasites “wreak havoc” in the guts of Autistic children every 29 days ( ABC7 News ) . This is astrology dressed as clinical protocol, and it has been sold to terrified parents as science.

Sign Petition 1

Sign Petition 2

The Philosophical And Ethical Rot At The Centre Of “Fake Cures”

Here is where I want to slow down, because the technical fraud is almost the least interesting part of this to me, the deeper violence is philosophical.

A “cure” for autism requires a prior claim; that Autistic existence is itself the pathology, the thing to be eliminated, rather than one configuration of a bodymind moving through a world built for someone else’s neurology. Every “cure” narrative smuggles in an ontology where the Autistic child, as they actually are, is understood as an absence, a “real” (implicitly non-Autistic) child trapped inside, injured, poisoned, and waiting to be extracted. Rivera’s own language (“removed from the spectrum,” “recovered”) depends entirely on this framing. It cannot exist without it.

This is where epistemic injustice, in Fricker’s sense, does its quiet work. Autistic people are testimonially discredited as narrators of our own existence before the conversation even starts, because the premise of “cure” culture requires that our lived, embodied Autistic experience be treated as noise generated by toxins, not as a legitimate way of being a person. The parent is positioned as the only credible witness, the child is positioned as evidence of damage. Nobody in that room is listening to what an Autistic child’s distress or joy might actually be trying to communicate, because the protocol has already decided what it is; parasites, heavy metals, vaccine injury, anything except a person.

That’s the ethical crime underneath the biochemical one. Before anyone administers a single dose, the ideology has already erased the child as a legitimate subject.

The Evidence Base That Doesn’t Exist

There isn’t one. This needs to be said plainly and repeatedly, because “controversial” and “alternative” get used by media coverage in ways that imply a genuine scientific disagreement. There isn’t one. There have never been any clinical trials, and neither Humble nor Rivera (who is a real estate agent, not a doctor) have cited any studies supporting their claims ( Altogether Autism ).

Regulatory and public health bodies across multiple countries have independently reached the same conclusion. Formal statements against chlorine dioxide/bleach therapy have been issued by bodies including the Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry, and the FDA repeatedly since 2010, alongside equivalent warnings from health agencies in Brazil and the UK, and from the WHO. This is not one lone dissenting institution being cautious. This is the near-total consensus of every body whose job it is to evaluate exactly this kind of claim.

The Actual Physical Harm

The FDA has been direct about what ingesting this substance does to a human body. People who have ingested chlorine dioxide solutions have experienced severe vomiting, severe diarrhea, life-threatening low blood pressure, dehydration, and acute liver failure all signs of bleach poisoning. Wider reporting on associated products adds seizures and respiratory problems to that list. Poison control centres in the US alone managed more than 16,000 related cases over a five-year period, fifty of them life-threatening, and eight of them fatal ( NBC News ).

Sixteen thousand cases. Fifty life-threatening. Eight deaths. These figures cover general MMS use across all claimed applications; cancer, HIV, malaria, meaning the true count of Autistic children specifically harmed by the autism-targeted protocol sits somewhere inside that data, uncounted and unspecified, because nobody with power has thought it urgent enough to isolate.

The Trauma, And Who Actually Carries It

I want to widen the lens here, because most coverage of this stops at the child directly forced t

posts.title: NeuroHub Community At The ISPS International Congress in Lausanne, Switzerland
posts.excerpt: A week ago today myself and my fellow NeuroHub director Jonathan Towse were on a plan to Switzerland. This was being done so that I could present my seminar Autism, Psychosis, And The Ecology Of Distress at the international congress of the International Society For Psychological And Social Approaches To Psychosis (ISPS). The weather was […]
posts.text:
A week ago today myself and my fellow NeuroHub director Jonathan Towse were on a plan to Switzerland. This was being done so that I could present my seminar Autism, Psychosis, And The Ecology Of Distress at the international congress of the International Society For Psychological And Social Approaches To Psychosis (ISPS).

The weather was blisteringly hot, and the flight was cramped, but it was all worth it for the reception of my presentation (which was very well received) on an international stage. We made connections and shared idea that could do a great deal of good for those who we aim to serve.

Over the course of the seminar, I explored the cyclic nature of psychotic experiences for Autistic people; exploring idea’s like the Autistic Burnout-To-Psychosis cycle, as well as recontextualising burnout and distress through an ecosystemic model, rather than one built on symptomatic, medicalised terminology.

One interesting moment was when I was presented with a question of why I combat stigma through wearing my diagnoses as identities. My answer was simple:

Some aspects of my life are incredibly difficult, some are amazing, but underneath it all is the aggressive neutrality of being human, and I wanted people to see that neurodivergent life is just as neutral and mundane as anyone elses most of the time. Our lives do not need to be sensational.

Below is a selection of photo’s from our trip, including some beautiful images of the mountains and Lake Geneva. For those interested in attending my seminar in a webinar format, I am currently planning to deliver it again at the end of August, tickets are £5.

posts.title: A Mother’s Response
posts.excerpt: David’s mother responds to his rtecent article exploring his addiction.
posts.text:
The following is a response to my recent article entitled Reasons I should Have Seen My Addiction But Didn’t. With my mother’s permission, I am publishing it as I feel it could speak to other people in similar situations. The following was written by Rev. Betsy Gray-Hammond, and could be difficult to read for some people.

Dear David

I am going to begin this by telling you how incredibly proud I am of you. I don’t think I actually tell you enough and I love you to the moon and back.

As I said I would have to, I have read your latest and I can only imagine how difficult it was to put your story ‘out there’ . What I am going to say to you now is harder than I have ever thought it would be. Why? Because you speak of not seeing the signs and getting drawn further and further in until you couldn’t even remember how life was before your addiction started.

I knew you were in addiction long before it became “official” and I was always there on the sidelines, always ready to bail you out of rent issues, shortage of food, even on the day of your graduation using the money I had kept for official photos, to pay off your £200 library fine, the only way they would let you graduate.

To be honest I was surprised that you made it through, every day I was waiting for the knock on the door, every day I was waiting for a uniformed officer to tell how sorry they were that you had died, overdose , murder, accident. It was not just me that lived with this, it was Amber too, she was watching the big brother she idolised disappear before her eyes and we would both have laid down our lives for you.

You grew up in an area that was tough. You grew up as a beautifully funny, quirky child, one that didn’t like his ‘food touching’ there had to be a margin between each item on your plate and baked beans were always placed in isolation in a bowl at the side of your plate because they could not be contained on a plate or trusted not to contaminate other food.

School was murder for you. You were not like other children, you hated football, and still do. You could occasionally be encouraged to play Rugby, very rarely.

You danced

Played the trumpet

Sang in the church choir

You loved art and above all else science

You were an Altar server, even in your Goth Days , when, to the horror of some people you would don your white robe, whilst still wear, black nail varnish, eyeliner and blue black hair dye.

You were DIFFERENT and you paid the price… you were bullied by other kids, teachers and many others who should have known better.

You had to live in a house with your Grandma, DeeDee ( your Aunt) and myself. When you five I married a man I thought I would be with forever and allowed you to form a relationship with you, a short time after that you were joined by a baby sister, who you doted on, you loved helping to bath and dress her and you would always pick out the whitest frilliest clothes from her wardrobe with matching socks etc, ect.

To save your feelings , when your sister and I returned home I would put her in more practical clothing, changing her again in time to collect you from school, so you never guessed that she had not worn them all day.

My marriage broke down and you lost the only father you had ever really known. You took it all in your stride and just got on with it.

Living with wider family had much to do with my divorce, and this was not helped by my mum being disabled (spinal issues and COPD) and my sister, DeeDee, disabled and a drug addict. Something you said you would never do.

But the pressures or being different in a world that didn’t seem to care was going to change all of that.

And of course I noticed throughout your life your struggle to fit in a world that didn’t understand your needs, nor it seemed wanted to even try.

David is autistic, I said to so many childcare professionals the replies were stark, bland, and often downright rude.

You are an over anxious mother with too much knowledge of the subject, I was at this time an inclusion co-ordinator.

It’s your living situation

The birth of his sister has upset him

The arrival and departure of his stepfather ,why? His own couldn’t care less and was not part of his life.

He is not autistic, he just doesn’t like being told what to do

He just doesn’t concentrate, ( or you don’t know him like I do)

One of the best.. well the apple never falls far from the tree, this was the answer from a GP who seemed to think I was of a nervous disposition, just another hysterical mum

I promise I tried to find help, I tried to make life better and I should have noticed or perceived what would happen next.

I never saw much of you in your final year of college, I was at theological college, your sister had come with me, you wanted to remain at your college and your girlfriend.

You never said anything about voices, which I now know you were struggling with. You would visit when you could and enjoy Cuddesdon. I tried many times to encourage you to switch colleges and come back home, but you wanted to be you and had also, I now understand, a degree of PDA.

Then University appeared on the horizon, you were excited because Bradford had offered you an unconditional place and they were the best in your choice of Forensic Science.

Why did I let it happen, when did I take my eye off the ball. Had I not loved you enough, had you felt rejected and blamed me for your existence, all of these things spun through my head as I realised the trajectory your life was taking.

Freshers

Your first term was a wild one, you drank and made merry, or so I thought, but you were struggling with the busyness , the loudness and the fact that Uni was so peoplely. The boundaries within which you felt safe had gone, you were out there in a world that nothing other than early intervention could have helped.

As time went forward the plea for money came more often, my student loan is late.

I have spent so much on books and stationary, I cannot afford food, my mates are going out I cannot afford to go with them, Im stuck, insert location here, and need to get back to halls, these pleas extended slowly until we reached, ‘I cannot pay my rent’

You spoke of lectures, of practical’s, of burying dead pigs in all different ways to match crime scene possibilities to see how fast they decayed, of beetles that could strip bones clean. You had changed though, you could lie on the phone, you couldn’t ever face to face, and still cannot.

You became more distant, you needed more and more money and in my study one day I said to Amber, I think David is on drugs… we had a huge row, she demanded to know why I thought this, told me you never would and that I was totally and unequivocally wrong!

The world kept turning without a care as to what it was doing to you, I still fought for you, because I loved you,

By the time you came to your final year, I knew what was happening, but I had hoped that returning home would help. I was so naïve.

We never got the photos of your

posts.title: Ways I Should Have Seen My Addiction But Didn’t
posts.excerpt: When we think about Autistic and/or ADHD people trapped in cycles of addiction, we rarely consider the real experiences that come with it. This article takes a look at the raw, unfiltered, and often harrowing experiences that we change the meaning of to justify our addictive behaviour.
posts.text:
There is a particular cruelty to addiction. Not just the physical toll, not just the destruction it leaves in its wake, but the way it makes catastrophe feel ordinary. Looking back now, I can see a trail of moments that should have stopped me cold. Moments that, in another life, might have prompted me to ask for help.

Instead, I rationalised every single one.

This post is not an easy one to write. But I think it’s an important one, because if you’re in the thick of it right now, you might recognise yourself here. If you do, I want you to know; the signs were always there. You just couldn’t see them yet, I couldn’t either.

Content note: This post contains references to substance use, overdose, violence, gang involvement, and housing instability.

The Tactical Chunder

We called it “tactical”. Making ourselves sick throughout the night to create more capacity for drink and drugs. It felt like a funny quirk, a practical solution, a thing we laughed about.

It was not funny.

It was not practical.

It was a bodymind screaming for relief and a group of people so deep in their using that this had simply become procedure.

I didn’t hear the scream, I just thought we were clever.

“How Are You Not Dead Yet?”

People said this to me regularly. Not as a joke, or at least, not entirely as a joke. They had witnessed what I was consuming; the quantities, the combinations, the frequency.
I heard it as a compliment, a testament to my constitution, I believed it was a badge of honour.

What it actually was; people who cared about me, terrified and not knowing how else to say so. They were watching me die by increments and reaching for humour because nothing else was working.

I was too busy feeling proud to notice.

The Quantities That Would Have Ended My Freedom

At various points I was buying hard drugs in quantities that, had the police caught me, could have resulted in a sentence that took the rest of my life.

I was proud when I got away with it. I felt invincible, I experienced getting away from the police as an achievement rather than as the desperately close call it was. The bravado was the point, the danger was invisible.

The Kidnapping

I was once kidnapped by a cocaine dealer. I had to set off a makeshift firework to escape.
I don’t say this for shock value, I say it because at the time, I filed it away as a story, something to tell.

Something that had happened to me and that I had survived, therefore it was proof of my resilience rather than evidence of how far things had gone.

When your life is endangered and your first thought is “this will make a good anecdote”, that is not resilience. That is dissociation from the reality of what you are living.

The Weapons

I was deeply enough embedded in drug gang life that I thought nothing of carrying deadly weapons on my person for protection. There was a logic to it, a logic that felt entirely coherent from inside.

I also knew, somewhere in the back of my mind, that there was a real chance I might use them one day.
I told myself this was just survival, what it was, was a life lived so far outside of safety that violence had become a calculated risk I was willing to accept.

Dealing To Fund Using

At various points I was dealing substances to fund my own use. The circular logic of it felt almost elegant at the time, it solved a problem.
What it actually meant was that my using had escalated beyond what I could sustain financially, and rather than recognise that as the crisis it was, I found a workaround. Addiction is extraordinarily creative when it comes to workarounds.

Never Having Enough For Rent

I never had enough money to cover my rent, not because I wasn’t working. Because every available resource was being routed toward substances.

There is something particularly telling about this one, because rent is a baseline. It is the minimum of keeping yourself housed and alive. I consistently could not meet it, I treated this as a logistical inconvenience rather than what it was; my life being consumed.

Trap Houses And Abandoned Buildings

I moved in and out of trap houses and abandoned buildings. I told myself it was practical, saving money, being resourceful.

The reality was I was sacrificing the safety and stability of housing, one of the most fundamental of human needs, to ensure I had enough for drugs. I had reorganised the entire hierarchy of my needs around the addiction.

Extracting Codeine

I was extracting codeine from paracetamol using imperfect equipment. I knew what I was doing to my body, I knew the risk, I did it anyway, because I needed the fix.

The knowledge of the harm was not a deterrent. It barely registered, that is the nature of dependency, the knowing and the doing exist in different compartments, and the doing always wins.

I was diagnosed with cirrhosis of the liver this year. This was said to be one of the likely culprits.

Moving 300 Miles To Escape

I had to uproot my entire life and move 300 miles away to escape gang members I had wronged.

Think about that for a moment, my using had embedded me so deeply in a world of organised crime that the only viable exit from a threat to my life was geographic displacement. I left a place, a life, relationships, everything; because staying was too dangerous.

I treated it as a fresh start, I didn’t treat it as evidence of the depth of the crisis I was in.

67 Overdoses In One Year

I overdosed on morphine 67 times in one year.

I don’t know how to add much to that.

It is a number that I still find difficult to sit with. Each one was survived, each one was normalised, each one became just another event in a year full of events. In fact i used to get angry if they tried to administer naloxone, the life saving drug that reverses opioid overdoses.

Sixty-seven times my body came close enough to death that it constituted a clinical overdose, and I kept going.

What Addiction Does To Perspective

The thread running through all of this is not stupidity, it is not weakness, it is not even denial in the way the word is usually deployed; as a kind of wilful blindness.

It is the way that addiction systematically reorganises your perception of what is normal, each escalation becomes the new baseline.

Each crisis that is survived becomes evidence that you are fine, the more extreme things get, the more ordinary they feel.

The absurd becomes quirky, the life-threatening becomes an anecdote. The catastrophic becomes an inconvenience.

I could not see the signs because I was living inside a reality that addiction had constructed for me. A reality where “tactical chunder” was funny, where 67 overdoses was just a bad year, where carrying weapons and moving to escape gangs were simply things that happened.

Recovery did not begin when the signs became visible, the signs were always there i could always see them. Recovery began when I could finally let them mean something.

I celebrated 10 years of recovery this year.

Autistic Mental Health Conference

Professional

posts.title: Not a Psychopath (Part 1): How Autism, Alexithymia and Trauma Get Misread
posts.excerpt: Autism, alexithymia, trauma and impulsivity can look like psychopathy from the outside. Here is why that misreading harms Autistic people, and why context matters. (Part 1).
posts.text:
A thought has been quietly nagging at one of us for a while, and we suspect that we are not the only neurodivergent people to have entertained it. The thought runs like this;

Perhaps a good deal of what our culture labels “psychopathy” actually describes a particular combination of more familiar neurodivergent ingredients.

You take autism, you add alexithymia, you add a body that seeks out internal sensation, and you stir in a generous measure of impulsivity. The result, viewed from the outside, can resemble the cold and calculating figure of psychopathy from popular imagination.

The idea tempts us because each ingredient corresponds to something real. The idea also turns out to be wrong in its strongest form, and the reasons it falls apart matter far more than the original hunch ever did. So, rather than abandon the thought quietly, we want to walk through it properly and together, because following it all the way to its conclusion reveals something genuinely important about how observers perceive Autistic people, how they misread us, and how that misreading causes real harm.

We write this piece in two voices and one argument. We agree on everything that matters, and between us we want to hold two truths at the same time. The overlap between psychopathy descriptors and neurodivergent experience represents one of the most dangerous diagnostic traps in the whole field; the answer, however, is not to swing so far in the opposite direction that we dismiss psychopathy as a construct or imply that anyone who presents with callous-unemotional traits must “really” be something else. That overcorrection would create its own kind of harm. The truth lives in the nuance, and the nuance, as we will argue throughout, lives in the ecosystem.

Where The Autism and Alexithymia Hunch Comes From

We should begin by treating the intuition fairly, because it does not rest on nothing. The overlap between autism and alexithymia is both real and substantial. Alexithymia describes a difficulty identifying and describing one’s own emotions, paired with an externally oriented thinking style, and it sits at the very centre of Autistic experience rather than at its edges. Estimates vary, yet researchers commonly cite figures in the region of forty to sixty-five percent, and “severe” alexithymia appears far more often within the Autistic community than in the general population (Kinnaird et al., 2019; Poquérusse et al., 2018). One systematic review and meta-analysis placed the prevalence at roughly fifty percent in Autistic groups, compared with around five percent in non-Autistic comparison groups (Kinnaird et al., 2019). This pattern represents one of the most robust findings in the entire area, and it reflects something structural rather than coincidental.

We need to be precise about what alexithymia actually is, because the precision changes everything. Alexithymia describes a difficulty accessing and naming emotion, and it does not describe an absence of emotion. The feeling is genuinely there, and sometimes it overwhelms the person entirely. The feeling simply cannot reach verbal processing, cannot reach outward expression, and frequently cannot even reach the person’s own conscious awareness in the moment. From the outside, an observer therefore sees flat affect, apparent unconcern, an absence of expected distress, and what looks like a failure to care. From the inside, a storm rages, and the storm cannot get out in any way that other people expect or recognise. One could be forgiven for seeing an overlap between the presentation of Autistic alexithymia and the flat and shameless affect of the psychopath.

This finding produced something even more significant. Bird and Cook (2013) proposed what researchers now call the “alexithymia hypothesis,” which argues that co-occurring alexithymia explains many of the emotional-processing difficulties that clinicians long assumed belonged to autism itself. This position carries real weight rather than fringe status; a growing body of work demonstrates that once researchers account for alexithymia, many of the supposed empathy “deficits” in Autistic people shrink dramatically or vanish completely. Difficulties that clinicians once treated as hallmarks of autism, including poor recognition of emotional facial expressions and atypical interoception, actually track with alexithymia rather than with autism (Cook et al., 2013; Shah et al., 2016).

This evidence reframes the cultural stereotypes about autism almost entirely. The familiar claims, that Autistic people lack empathy, that we struggle with emotional reciprocity, and that we cannot read or share feelings, turn out to describe alexithymia rather than autism, because alexithymia travels alongside autism while remaining a distinct experience (Poquérusse et al., 2018). The “severe” combination of alexithymia and autism has unfortunately become the cultural archetype that stands in for autism as a whole. Picture the fictional characters that most people reach for when they imagine an Autistic person, and you will usually find portraits of that specific “severe” co-occurrence rather than portraits of autism in general.

Milton’s double empathy problem (2012) takes this insight further and points us toward the argument that anchors this whole piece. The empathy gap runs in both directions at once; neurotypical observers fail to read and understand the Autistic person’s emotional world just as surely as the reverse, so what gets named as a “lack of empathy” usually describes a mismatch between two different ways of being rather than a moral absence inside one person. That distinction matters enormously, and it gives us the first clear sign that the failure to connect does not sit inside the Autistic person alone.

Interoceptive differences in how the body processes, integrates and understands its own internal signals appear commonly in Autistic people (Price & Hooven, 2018; Shah et al., 2016). Sign-Up For Professional Gateway

From there, the trio works through three central questions. What do we actually mean when we say neuroaffirming, and does it mean the same thing to everyone? Can neuroaffirming practice be done badly, including by organisations that use the term as a marketing buzzword without backing it up? And finally, is there something beyond neuroaffirming we should be striving for; leading David to introduce the idea of neurodivergent competence, building on Tanya Adkin’s work on monotropic split and the monotropic spiral, and to ask what genuine competence in supporting neurodivergent people would actually require.

Along the way the discussion touches on where affirmation meets ethical complexity, who gets to claim authority on neurodivergent experience, and why genuine dialogue and listening matter more than credentials.

The episode closes with details of NeuroHub’s online Stim & Glimmer Party for Autistic Pride, and a final round of “glimmers”; the small things bringing everyone joy that week.
